learn: Families come in many shapes: joint, nuclear, single-parent, adoptive, grandparents raising children. None is the 'real' one.

Families share work. Who does which job at home is a choice, not a law of nature.

deep.q: What makes a group of people a family?
deep.why: Every society has families, but they are built very differently. Some count relatives through the mother's line, some through the father's, some through both. Some children are raised by a whole village. Asking what makes a family is asking what holds people together at all.
views: Biology
Family is shared genes: parents, children and their blood relatives. This explains inherited looks and traits, but not adopted children, step-parents or chosen family.
Kerala's matrilineal Nair and Meghalaya's Khasi traditions
Family and property pass through the mother's line. Among the Khasi, the youngest daughter traditionally inherits the house. So 'who is family' depends on which line a society follows.
Care-based view
Family is whoever cares for you day after day. A grandmother raising a child, or two friends who share a home for life, can be family.
deep.tryit: Make two lists: people related to you by birth, and people who look after you. Where do the lists overlap? Who is on only one list, and are they less your family?

deep.q: Why does Hindi have chacha, mama, fufa and mausa where English has only 'uncle'?
deep.why: Languages grow words for what a culture needs to tell apart. In joint families it mattered whether an uncle was from your father's side (who might live with you) or your mother's side (who usually didn't).
views: Linguists
Kinship words show how a society organises duties: who you live with, who inherits, who you may marry.
English speakers
One word is simpler, and the difference can be explained when needed ('my mother's brother').
Tamil
Tamil goes further: an older brother (annan) and younger brother (thambi) have different words, because age order carries different roles.
deep.tryit: Ask an elder for every relative's name in your home language. Count them. Then count the English words for the same people.

deep.q: Do animals have families and friends, or are we just imagining it?
deep.why: It is easy to see human feelings in animals. Scientists try hard not to, so the evidence matters.
views: Elephant researchers
Herds are led by the oldest female, who remembers water holes from decades before. Herds with older matriarchs survive droughts better.
Primatologists
Chimpanzees and baboons form long friendships, groom friends more, and are calmer near them.
Careful sceptics
We should not call it 'friendship' unless it is more than just staying near someone. What we can measure is choosing, helping and returning to the same individual.
deep.tryit: Watch a group of pigeons, crows or street dogs for 10 minutes. Do some always stay together? What would count as proof that two are friends?

deep.q: Is bargaining fair?
deep.why: At a mela, prices are often not fixed. The buyer wants it cheap; the seller wants enough to live on. Bargaining is an old way of finding a price both accept, but it can also be unequal.
views: The haggler
Bargaining is a game of respect: both sides talk and meet in the middle.
The artisan
If customers always push the price down, the person who made the thing by hand for days may not earn enough. Fair-trade shops fix prices to protect makers.
Economists
A fair price is one both sides accept freely, knowing the facts. Bargaining is fair when both know what the thing is really worth.
deep.tryit: Play shop: one person makes a paper toy and must earn at least ₹20 worth of tokens for it. The other has ₹30. Bargain. Then swap roles. How did each side feel?

deep.q: Why do so many melas happen just after harvest?
deep.why: Melas are tied to the farming calendar. After harvest, farmers have money, food and free time, and the weather is often pleasant.
views: Historians
Fairs like Sonepur and Pushkar grew from cattle and camel trading at set times each year, when animals and crops could be sold.
Religious traditions
Many melas mark a festival or a holy bath (like the Kumbh), so the date comes from the stars and the Moon.
Today
Some melas are now planned for tourists. Does that change what a mela is?
deep.tryit: Pick three melas (Pushkar, Surajkund, a local one). Find the month each happens and what farmers are doing at that time.

deep.q: Is a mela a kind of living thing?
deep.why: A mela appears, grows, draws in energy (people, money, food), changes, ends, and comes back next year. Thinking about this tests what we mean by 'alive'.
views: Biologists
No: a mela has no cells and does not reproduce or evolve by itself.
Systems thinkers
Cities, markets and ant colonies behave like living systems: many parts following simple rules make something bigger that seems to have a life of its own.
Oneness traditions
Thousands of people moving as one, then scattering and gathering again, is a picture of how separate selves are part of one larger life.

deep.q: Why does Diwali move around the calendar but Christmas doesn't?
deep.why: People have always used the sky to keep time. The Sun gives the year and the seasons; the Moon gives months of about 29½ days. The two don't fit neatly: 12 lunar months are about 11 days shorter than a solar year.
views: The solar calendar (used for Christmas and the school year)
Follows the Sun, so dates stay with the seasons.
The Hindu lunisolar calendar (Panchang)
Months follow the Moon, but an extra month (adhik maas) is added about every three years so festivals stay in the right season. That's why Diwali always comes in autumn but on different dates.
The Islamic calendar
Purely lunar with no extra month, so Eid moves through all the seasons over about 33 years.
deep.tryit: Find the dates of Diwali and Eid for the last 5 years. Which moves more? Can you explain why from the rules above?

deep.q: Should festivals change when they harm others?
deep.why: Festivals carry meaning across generations. But some customs (loud firecrackers, plastic decorations, idols in rivers) affect air, water, animals and people with breathing problems.
views: Tradition keepers
Customs connect us to our grandparents and give the festival its meaning; changing them loses something.
Environmental scientists
Firecrackers add fine dust that can make city air much worse for days; animals and birds are frightened by the noise.
Many communities
Festivals have always changed. Clay idols, green crackers, community diyas and quiet hours are new traditions keeping the old meaning.
deep.tryit: Ask three elders how their festivals were celebrated as children. What changed, and why? Was the change for better or worse?

deep.q: Do animals and plants have festivals?
deep.why: In spring, birds sing and nest; in the monsoon, frogs gather and call all night; some flowers bloom together on one night. These are timed by the season, like many human festivals.
views: Ecologists
These are 'phenology': life events timed by day length, temperature and rain. Many human festivals are also tied to these same cycles, such as harvest festivals.
Poets and many traditions
The koel's call announcing spring has been celebrated for centuries as nature's own festival.
Careful thinkers
A festival needs meaning and choice. Do frogs choose, or only respond? What is the difference?

deep.q: Do plants move, sense and decide?
deep.why: Plants seem still only because they are slow. Time-lapse films show shoots circling, roots bending towards water, leaves following the Sun. J.C. Bose built instruments to record plant responses over a century ago.
views: Plant scientists
Plants sense light, gravity, touch, chemicals and damage, and respond, all without a brain or nerves. Roots grow downward because special cells sense gravity.
'Plant intelligence' researchers
Some argue plants learn and remember (the touch-me-not stops folding when repeatedly dropped harmlessly).
Critics
Words like 'decide' and 'learn' may be too human. Responding is not the same as thinking.

deep.q: Is a tree one living thing or a whole city?
deep.why: A big tree is home to insects, birds, lichens, fungi and microbes. Its roots partner with fungi that bring water and minerals in exchange for sugar.
views: Ecologists
A tree is a keystone: remove it and many species lose their homes.
The 'wood wide web' idea
Some scientists say trees share sugar and warnings through fungal networks under the soil.
Recent critics (2023)
Other scientists reviewed the evidence and said those claims are often exaggerated; the fungi certainly connect roots, but whether trees 'help each other' is unproven.
deep.tryit: Choose one tree. In 15 minutes, count every other living thing you can find on or under it.

deep.q: Why did Saalumarada Thimmakka call trees her children?
deep.why: Thimmakka of Karnataka, who had no children of her own, planted and watered hundreds of banyan saplings along a highway, carrying water for kilometres. She was awarded the Padma Shri.
views: Science
A banyan can live for centuries and support whole communities of creatures; planting one is one of the longest-lasting gifts a person can give.
Many Indian traditions
Trees like the peepal, banyan and tulsi are treated as sacred and cared for like family.
Your view
Can you love a tree? Can a tree be family? What would you need to do for it?
deep.tryit: Adopt one tree for a month: name it, measure its trunk with string, give it water in summer, and record its visitors.

learn: A habitat gives food, water and shelter. Trees, ponds and even cracks in walls are habitats.
Plants and animals depend on each other: bees and bats carry pollen, birds and animals spread seeds, earthworms enrich soil, plants feed and shelter animals.
Food chains: grass is eaten by a deer, a deer by a tiger. Decomposers (fungi, worms, bacteria) return everything to the soil.
The baya weaver: the male weaves a hanging nest of grass; the female inspects it and chooses.
Remove one living thing and others feel it; that's why forests with many kinds of life recover better.
think: Who needs whom more: the bee or the flower?
If all mosquitoes vanished, would that be good? Some scientists think little would change; others say fish, birds and bats would lose food. What do you think?
Is a weed bad? Who decides which plant is a weed?
x.oneness: A tree feeds the bird, the bird spreads the tree's seeds, the worm feeds the tree. If each needs the others, is a forest one big living being?
jokes: Why don't ants get sick? They have tiny anty-bodies!
Why did the bee get married? It found its honey!
What did the tree say to the woodpecker? Leaf me alone!
quiz: The male baya weaver builds the nest.
The female chooses which nest she likes.
Bats can pollinate flowers.

Earthworms make soil better for plants.
Their tunnels let in air and their waste is rich food for plants.
Animals never help plants.
They pollinate, spread seeds and enrich soil.
odd: Bees, butterflies and bats can all carry pollen.
ws: Draw 6 living things and connect them with arrows. Write on each arrow what is given.
Match: frog, baya, earthworm, monkey, fish → pond, tree, soil, river, palm tree.

deep.q: Who needs whom more: the bee or the flower?
deep.why: Bees get nectar and pollen as food; flowers get their pollen carried to other flowers so they can make seeds. Neither gives on purpose, yet both depend on the other. This is called mutualism.
views: Ecologists
Many crops (mangoes, apples, almonds, many vegetables) depend heavily on pollinators; without them, harvests fall sharply.
Evolution biologists
Flowers and pollinators shaped each other over millions of years: long tubes and long tongues, bright colours and colour vision.
A deeper question
If neither could exist without the other for long, are they two things or one partnership?
deep.tryit: Sit by a flowering plant for 10 minutes. Count the visitors. Do different insects visit different flowers?

deep.q: If all mosquitoes disappeared, would that be good?
deep.why: Mosquitoes spread malaria and dengue, which kill many people each year. But they are also food for fish, frogs, birds and bats, and some pollinate plants.
views: Some scientists
Most mosquito species are not harmful to people, and other insects could fill their role; removing the few disease-carrying species could save many lives.
Other ecologists
Mosquito larvae are a big food source in ponds and the Arctic; removing them could have effects we can't predict.
Ethicists
Do humans have the right to wipe out a species, even a harmful one?
deep.tryit: Draw a food web around a pond with a mosquito in it. Cross it out. Which arrows break?

deep.q: Who decides what a 'weed' is?
deep.why: A weed is just a plant growing where a person doesn't want it. Many 'weeds' are medicines, food for insects or the first plants to heal damaged soil.
views: Farmers
Weeds compete with crops for water and light and lower the harvest.
Ecologists
Wild plants feed bees and butterflies and hold soil together.
Ayurveda and folk medicine
Plants like 'doob' grass and 'punarnava' are used as medicines.
deep.tryit: Find three 'weeds' near your home. Learn their names. Is any of them useful to an insect, a bird or a person?

learn: Living in harmony means sharing space and resources fairly with people and with nature.
Disagreeing is normal. Listening, taking turns and finding a fix both sides accept is a skill you can practise.
When forests shrink, animals come into towns and farms (monkeys, elephants, leopards). It isn't only the animals' fault.
People have found clever ways to share: beehive fences keep elephants out of farms because elephants avoid bees.
The Bishnoi community and the Chipko movement protected trees with their own bodies.
think: When a monkey snatches food in a town, who is the real problem: the monkey, or the people who took its forest?
Is it always good to agree? Can disagreeing kindly lead to better ideas?
Contrary view: people often say nature is 'in balance'. Many ecologists say nature is always changing, never perfectly balanced. Which seems true where you live?
x.oneness: If you dirty the river, the river comes back to you as water. Can you hurt nature without hurting yourself?
jokes: Why did the two trees stop arguing? They agreed to leaf it!
What do you call a peaceful dinosaur? A calm-asaurus!
Why do bees hum? They forgot the words!
quiz: Beehive fences can keep elephants away from farms.
Elephants avoid bees.
The Chipko movement was about hugging trees to stop them being cut.
It began in the hills of Uttarakhand in the 1970s.
Living in harmony means never disagreeing.
It means disagreeing kindly and finding fair fixes.
Animals come into towns only because they are naughty.
Often their homes and food have been taken.
odd: The other three help people get along.

deep.q: When a monkey steals food in town, whose fault is it?
deep.why: As forests shrink and food is left in the open, monkeys, elephants and leopards come into towns. People feel the animals are the problem; the animals are following food and space.
views: Wildlife biologists
Feeding monkeys teaches them to depend on people and become bolder; most conflict starts with food we leave or give.
Farmers near forests
Losing a harvest to elephants can ruin a family; they need protection and compensation.
Solutions that worked
Beehive fences keep elephants away because elephants avoid bees; covered dustbins and not feeding monkeys reduce raids.
deep.tryit: Write the same event (a monkey grabbing a banana) twice: once as the person, once as the monkey. What does each one need?

deep.q: Is nature 'in balance'?
deep.why: People often say nature is in perfect balance until humans upset it. It is a comforting idea, but is it true?
views: Older ecology
Nature tends towards a stable balance where each species has its place.
Modern ecology
Nature is always changing: fires, floods, droughts and new species keep shifting things. 'Balance' is more like a dance than a still scale.
A middle view
Even if nature changes, human changes are now so fast and so big that many species can't keep up.
deep.tryit: Look at old photos of your area from 30 years ago (ask elders). What changed? Which changes were natural, which human?

deep.q: Can people who disagree live in harmony?
deep.why: Harmony in music is different notes sounding good together, not everyone singing the same note. India has hundreds of languages, foods and faiths living side by side.
views: Peacemakers
Harmony comes from listening and finding fair rules, not from everyone agreeing.
Philosophers
Disagreement, done kindly, helps everyone think better.
Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
If the world is one family, quarrels are family quarrels; you still belong together after them.
deep.tryit: Next time you disagree with someone at home, each of you repeats the other's view in your own words before replying. Did it change anything?

learn: Water comes from rain, rivers, lakes, glaciers and under the ground (groundwater, reached by wells and borewells).
Most of Earth's water is salty sea water. Only about 3 in every 100 drops is fresh, and most of that is frozen; very little is easy for us to use.
The water cycle: the sun heats water, vapour rises, cools into clouds, falls as rain, flows back to rivers and seas.
Dirty water spreads diseases; boiling, filtering and clean storage make water safer.
India's traditional water-keepers: stepwells (baolis), johads, kunds and temple tanks stored rain for dry months.
think: Who owns the rain that falls on your roof? Who owns a river?
If Earth is covered in water, why do cities run short?
Contrary view: is bottled water always safer than tap water? (Not always, and the bottles make plastic waste.) How could a family decide?
x.oneness: The water in your body was once a cloud, a river, maybe a dinosaur's drink. Are you a small walking river?
jokes: What did the ocean say to the beach? Nothing, it just waved!
How do you save water? In a piggy bucket!
Why did the cloud go to school? To learn how to rain on parade!
quiz: Most of Earth's water is salty.
About 97 of every 100 drops are in the seas.
Groundwater is water stored under the ground.
Wells and borewells reach it.
Muddy water that looks clear after filtering is always safe to drink.
Germs can still be there; boil it.
Stepwells were built to store water for dry months.
Many are hundreds of years old.

Who owns the rain? Write what you think and why.

deep.q: Who owns the rain?
deep.why: Water falls freely from the sky, but rivers, wells and pipes are shared by many people, farms, factories, animals and other states. Deciding who gets how much is one of the biggest questions of our time.
views: The law in India
Water in rivers and under the ground is treated as a shared public resource that governments manage for everyone.
Farmers upstream and downstream
Rivers like the Kaveri are shared by states that have argued about them for over a hundred years.
Traditional communities
Johads, kunds and stepwells were built and cared for by whole villages; water belonged to the community that kept it.
deep.tryit: Find where your home's water comes from (tap, tanker, well, river). Who else uses that same source?

deep.q: If Earth is covered in water, why do people run short?
deep.why: About 97 of every 100 drops on Earth are salty sea water. Of the fresh 3, most is frozen in ice or deep underground. Only a tiny part is in rivers, lakes and reachable groundwater.
views: Hydrologists
India pumps more groundwater than any other country; in many places it is being used faster than rain refills it.
Engineers
Desalination (removing salt from sea water) can help but uses a lot of energy.
Water harvesters
Catching rain where it falls, on roofs and in ponds, can refill the ground.
deep.tryit: Do the apple model: cut an apple into 4 (three quarters are the sea), and keep cutting the last piece to see how small the usable fresh water is.

deep.q: Is water ever really 'new'?
deep.why: The water on Earth has been recycling for billions of years: evaporating, raining, flowing, frozen, drunk and breathed out.
views: Science
The same water molecules may have passed through clouds, oceans, plants and animals, including dinosaurs, many times.
Many Indian traditions
Rivers are honoured as mothers (Ganga Maa) because they carry life from the mountains to us.
Oneness
If the water in you was once a cloud and will be a river again, where do you end and the water cycle begin?
deep.tryit: Breathe on a cold mirror. Where did that water come from, and where will it go next?

Your bottle filter made muddy water look clear. Is it safe to drink now? Why or why not? What else would you do?
Who owns the rain that falls on your roof? Who owns a river? Write what you think and why.

learn: Food comes from plants (grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, spices) and animals (milk, eggs, fish, meat).
Each region eats what grows nearby: coconut and rice in Kerala, wheat in Punjab, fish in Bengal, millets in dry lands.
Millets (ragi, bajra, jowar) grow with little water and are very nutritious; 2023 was the International Year of Millets.
Cooking changes food: taste, softness, colour, and sometimes how easily the body can use it.
A balanced plate has energy foods, body-building foods and protective foods.
think: Is rice better than millet? Better for whom: your body, the farmer, the river?
Why do people in different places eat such different foods?
Two sides: some say vegetarian food is healthiest; others say eggs or fish help growth. Many nutrition scientists say both can be healthy when balanced. What would you need to know to decide?
x.oneness: Sunlight grew the mango, and now the mango becomes you. Where does the food stop and you begin?
jokes: Why did the tomato blush? It saw the salad dressing!
What does a nervous laddoo say? I'm falling to pieces!
Why did the roti go to school? To be well-rounded!
quiz: Ragi and bajra are millets.
So are jowar and foxtail millet.
All food comes from plants.
Milk and eggs come from animals.
Potatoes contain starch.
Iodine turns them blue-black.
People everywhere eat the same food.
Food depends on what grows nearby and on culture.

deep.q: Rice or millet: which is better?
deep.why: Millets like ragi, bajra and jowar were India's main grains for thousands of years. Rice and wheat took over after the 1960s Green Revolution, which helped feed India but used much more water.
views: Nutritionists
Ragi is rich in calcium; bajra in iron. Millets also have more fibre than polished rice.
Farmers and water experts
Rice needs a lot of water; millets grow in dry land with little rain. That's why the UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets.
Cooks and families
Taste, habit and what's in the shop matter too. 'Better' depends on whether you mean for your body, the farmer or the river.
deep.tryit: Taste a ragi roti or ragi porridge and a rice dish. Compare taste, how full you feel, and look up how much water each crop needs.

deep.q: Why do people in different places eat such different food?
deep.why: Food follows land and climate: coconuts and rice in wet Kerala, wheat in Punjab, fish in Bengal and Goa, millets in dry Rajasthan. Trade, religion and history add more layers.
views: Geographers
What grows nearby shapes what people cook.
Historians
Chillies, potatoes and tomatoes came to India from the Americas only about 400–500 years ago; Indian food has always mixed and changed.
Today
Supermarkets bring food from everywhere. Is that good for farmers near you?
deep.tryit: Pick one dish your family cooks. List each ingredient and where it grows. How many came from far away?

deep.q: Vegetarian, eggs, fish or meat: what's healthiest?
deep.why: Families eat differently for reasons of health, belief, culture, cost and care for animals.
views: Many nutrition scientists
Both vegetarian and non-vegetarian diets can be healthy when balanced; pulses, milk, nuts and grains together give good protein.
Ethical vegetarians (and Jain and many Hindu traditions)
Avoiding harm to animals (ahimsa) is the main reason.
Coastal and hill communities
Fish, eggs or meat are local, affordable and traditional.
deep.tryit: Without judging, ask three people why they eat what they eat. Sort the reasons: health, belief, taste, cost, habit.

Which of these is a millet?

Is your plate balanced?
Trace three foods back to where they grew.

x.guide: Food is biology, geography and family history on one plate. Trace food back to farms and grandmothers' kitchens. Use your own regional dishes as the main examples, not textbook ones. Pitfall: iodine stains and isn't food. Use old cut pieces and throw them away after.

learn: Clean hands stop germs spreading: soap and 20 seconds of scrubbing remove far more than water alone.
Children aged 6–12 need about 9–12 hours of sleep. Growing and remembering happen while you sleep.
Playing and moving make the heart and lungs stronger and help feelings settle.
Feelings are signals. Naming them and talking about them helps.
Most microbes are harmless or helpful; only some make us sick.

Are all germs bad?

Pepper on water flees a soapy finger. Be honest: this shows soap changing the water's surface tension; it is a picture of handwashing, not proof of killing germs.

deep.q: Are germs our enemies?
deep.why: Germs (microbes) are everywhere: in soil, food, air and inside us. Only a small number cause disease. Our gut alone has trillions of helpful microbes.
views: Doctors
Handwashing with soap is one of the cheapest ways to prevent illness; soap lifts away the oils that hold germs.
Microbiologists
Many microbes are our helpers: they make curd, digest food and train our body's defences.
The 'hygiene hypothesis'
Some scientists think children who play outdoors and around animals develop fewer allergies; others say it's more about the right microbes than about dirt.
deep.tryit: Make curd at home. Which tiny living things made it? Are they 'germs'?

deep.q: Is happiness something you feel or something you do?
deep.why: Feelings come and go like weather. People have long asked whether we can grow lasting contentment.
views: Psychologists
Sleep, movement, time outdoors, friends and helping others reliably make people feel better.
Yoga and Buddhist traditions
Watching your breath and thoughts calmly builds a steady happiness that doesn't depend on getting things.
Philosophers
Some say a good life includes sadness too, and that feeling every feeling is healthy.
deep.tryit: For a week, write one thing that made you happy each day. Was it something you got, or something you did?

deep.q: Are mind and body two things or one?
deep.why: When you're scared your heart races; when you're tired you feel grumpy; when you laugh your body relaxes.
views: Modern science
The brain is part of the body, and hormones and nerves connect feelings and health both ways.
Descartes (a French thinker, 1600s)
Mind and body are two different kinds of things.
Vedanta
Body and mind are both layers (koshas) around a deeper Self; the true 'I' is the awareness that knows them both.
deep.tryit: Sit quietly for one minute and count your breaths. Then think of something scary. Did your breathing change? Who noticed the change?

wsd.p: Tick each day this week.

opts: It lifts away oil and dirt that hold germs

c.covers: Objects around us and what they are made of, natural vs human-made materials, properties like hard, soft, waterproof, magnetic.
game: Material Top Trumps

Make 20 cards of household objects and score each for hardness, bendiness, waterproofness and floating. Each turn, pick a property from your top card; the higher score wins both cards. Test any disputed score for real before deciding.
exp: Raincoat test: drip water on paper, plastic, cotton, wool and foil. Which keep a tissue underneath dry?
Magnet hunt: which things in the house does a magnet pick up? Are all metals magnetic?
act: 'Made of what?' house hunt: find 5 things each of wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth and clay.
Old vs new: compare a clay pot and a plastic bottle for keeping water cool.
proj: Material Museum

A museum display the child guides visitors through
read: The Way Things Work Now, David Macaulay (for parent and child together)

learn: Every object is made of one or more materials: wood, metal, glass, clay, plastic, cloth, paper, rubber.
Materials have properties: hard or soft, rough or smooth, see-through or not, waterproof or not, magnetic or not.
We choose materials for the job: glass for windows, rubber for tyres, steel for utensils.
Natural materials (wood, cotton, clay) come straight from nature; human-made ones (plastic, glass, steel) are made by changing natural ones.
Not all metals are magnetic: iron and steel stick to a magnet, aluminium, copper and gold don't.
think: A wooden chair: natural or human-made? Where is the line?
Why isn't a raincoat made of paper? What would you make it from if plastic didn't exist?
Two sides: plastic is often called bad, yet it also keeps medicines and hospital tools clean. When is plastic the right choice, and when not?
x.oneness: Your steel tumbler was once rock in the earth; your cotton shirt was a plant. Is anything really 'just a thing'?
jokes: What did the glass say to the plate? I can see right through you!
Why don't scientists trust atoms? They make up everything!
Why was the broom late? It over-swept!
quiz: All metals stick to a magnet.
Aluminium, copper and gold don't.
Glass is transparent.
You can see through it.
A clay pot can keep water cool.
Water seeps out and evaporates, taking heat with it.
Wood comes from trees.
It's the hard inside of trunks and branches.
odd: The others are made of metal.
ws: List 8 objects at home: material, one property, why that material.
Sort: cotton shirt, steel plate, wooden table, plastic bucket, clay pot, paper.
Design an umbrella for a hailstorm. Which materials and why?
Write one good use of plastic and one place we should stop using it.
hours: Activities: material house hunt, clay vs plastic
cur: ExpeRimental home science films (e.g. hidden colours in felt pens)
Separate the colours in one black pen with a strip of paper and water: one 'thing' made of many.

deep.q: Is anything really 'natural' or 'human-made'?
deep.why: A wooden chair is a tree shaped by people. Steel is iron ore from rock, changed by fire. Plastic is made from oil, which came from ancient living things.
views: Chemists
Everything is made of the same elements; humans only rearrange them.
Environmentalists
The difference matters: natural materials usually rot back into the earth; many human-made ones like plastic last for centuries.
Panchamahabhuta
Indian thought says all things are made of five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space.
deep.tryit: Take five objects. Trace each back to the earth: what was it before a person shaped it?

deep.q: Is plastic good or bad?
deep.why: Plastic is cheap, light, waterproof and long-lasting. Those same qualities make it a problem when thrown away.
views: Doctors
Sterile plastic syringes, drips and gloves save lives every day.
Ocean scientists
Millions of tonnes of plastic reach the sea every year, harming turtles, birds and fish, and breaking into tiny microplastics.
Designers
The question is not plastic or no plastic, but which uses are worth it and how we design things to be reused or recycled.
deep.tryit: Find ten plastic things at home. Mark each: needed, useful but replaceable, or not needed.

deep.q: Why is each thing made of the material it is?
deep.why: Engineers choose materials for their properties: glass windows let light through, rubber tyres grip and bend, clay pots cool water by letting it seep and evaporate.
views: Engineers
Choosing the wrong material makes things break, leak or burn.
Traditional craftspeople
Many old choices are clever science: matkas, bamboo houses and lime plaster suit Indian heat.
Inventors
New materials (like bioplastics from plants) keep changing what's possible.
deep.tryit: Pretend plastic was never invented. Redesign a water bottle, a raincoat and a toothbrush using other materials.

wsd.p: Test eight objects.
Sort these.
Which of these sticks to a magnet?
Raincoat test: drip water on each material over a tissue.
Design an umbrella for a hailstorm. Label each material and why you chose it.
Write one place plastic is the best choice and one place we should stop using it. Explain both.

x.guide: Everything is made of something, and each material was chosen for a reason. Your child becomes a materials tester. Let them predict before every test, and write predictions down. Wrong predictions are the best ones. Pitfall: not every metal is magnetic (steel spoons yes, aluminium foil no). Let them find this out.

learn: Artisans make things with skill: potters, weavers, carpenters, bamboo workers, blacksmiths.
Making follows steps: choose material, shape it, join or fire it, finish it.
Handmade vs factory-made: handmade items carry skill and variety; factories make many identical items cheaply.
Designers test and improve: first tries usually fail, and that's how good things are made.
Old things can be remade: cloth into quilts, bottles into planters, scraps into toys.
think: Who really makes a clay pot: the potter, the clay, the wheel or the fire?
Is handmade always better than factory-made?
Two sides: some say machines take artisans' jobs; others say machines make things cheaper for everyone. Can both be true?
x.oneness: A pot is earth shaped by hands, mixed with water, dried by air, hardened by fire, holding empty space. Earth, water, air, fire and space all made it together.
jokes: Why did the potter go to the party? For a wheel-y good time!
What did the hammer say to the nail? Get to the point!
Why did the paper go to the doctor? It felt torn!
quiz: A potter shapes clay on a wheel.
The wheel spins so the clay can be shaped evenly.
Bamboo can be used to build houses.
It is strong, light and grows fast.
Everything in shops is made by machines.
Many things are still handmade.
First designs usually work perfectly.
Designers test and improve again and again.
odd: The others make things with their hands.
ws: Number the steps of making a clay pot: fire it, dig clay, shape on wheel, dry in sun, knead with water.
Interview an artisan: what they make, tools, how long it takes, hardest part.
Sketch your toy. What happened at test 1, 2 and 3? What did you change?
Who made the pot? List everything that helped.

deep.q: Who really makes a clay pot?
deep.why: The potter shapes it, but the clay came from a riverbank, water softened it, the wheel spun it, the Sun dried it and fire hardened it.
views: Craftspeople
Skill passed down for generations is the real maker; a beginner with the same clay makes a lopsided pot.
Scientists
Fire changes the clay itself: above about 600°C, it becomes ceramic and can never turn back into soft clay.
Panchamahabhuta
Earth, water, air, fire and space (the hollow inside that makes it a pot) all work together.
deep.tryit: Shape a pot from dough or clay. List everything and everyone who helped make it.

deep.q: Is handmade better than factory-made?
deep.why: A handloom saree or a carved toy carries the maker's skill and is one of a kind. A factory makes thousands of identical things cheaply.
views: Artisans
Handmade work keeps traditions and livelihoods alive; India has millions of handloom weavers.
Economists
Factories make things affordable for many more people.
Designers
Some of the best things combine both: machines for the boring parts, hands for the skilled parts.
deep.tryit: Compare a handmade and a factory-made version of the same thing (a basket, a toy, cloth). Look closely and list differences.

deep.q: Why do good designs need failures?
deep.why: Almost nothing works perfectly the first time. Engineers build, test, fail, change and test again. This is called iteration.
views: Inventors
Thomas Edison's team tested thousands of materials for a bulb filament; each failure taught them something.
Indian frugal engineers
Jugaad, the knack of fixing things with what's at hand, is a kind of fast trial and error.
Scientists
A failed test is still data. The only real failure is not learning from it.
deep.tryit: Build a paper bridge that holds coins. Record each try: what broke, what you changed.

wsd.p: Match the maker to the tool.

Sketch your toy or bridge design. Label materials.
Record your tests.

learn: Waste can be wet (peels, leftover food), dry (paper, plastic, metal), hazardous (batteries, medicines) or e-waste (old phones).
Sorting at home makes recycling and composting possible.
Biodegradable things rot back into soil; plastic can last hundreds of years.
Reduce first, then reuse, then recycle. Composting turns wet waste into food for plants.
Kabadiwalas and waste-pickers recycle a large share of what India throws away.
think: When we 'throw away' something, where is 'away'?
Is a banana peel waste for a worm?
Two sides: some say recycling solves the problem; many experts say reducing what we use matters much more. Which is easier at your home?
x.oneness: In a forest every 'waste' becomes someone's food. What would your home look like if it worked like a forest?
jokes: What did the recycling bin say to the dustbin? You're such a waste!
Why was the bottle so happy? It got a second life!
Why did the banana peel go to the compost party? To break down on the dance floor!
quiz: Banana peels are biodegradable.
Microbes and worms turn them into soil.
Plastic bags break down in a few days.
They can last for hundreds of years.
Sorting waste at home helps recycling.
Clean dry waste can be recycled; wet waste can be composted.
Old batteries go in the wet-waste bin.
They are hazardous waste.
odd: The others can go into compost.
ws: Sort 12 things into wet, dry, hazardous and e-waste.
List everything your family threw away today. Which could have been avoided?
Draw 3 new uses for an old bottle.
Where is 'away'? Draw where your rubbish really goes.
hours: Activities: weigh a day's waste, talk to a kabadiwala
cur: Build two bottle composters; test which kitchen scraps rot fastest and measure the warmth.

deep.q: When we throw something 'away', where is 'away'?
deep.why: 'Away' is always somewhere: a landfill on a city's edge, a burning heap, a river, the sea, or a recycling yard. Delhi's Ghazipur landfill grew taller than a 20-storey building.
views: City planners
Landfills are running out of space; sorting at home is the cheapest fix.
Waste-pickers and kabadiwalas
They recover and recycle a large share of India's plastic and paper, often unrecognised.
Nature
In a forest there is no 'away': every leaf, dropping and dead body becomes food for something else.
deep.tryit: Follow one item (a bottle or a wrapper) after you bin it. Ask whoever collects your waste where it goes.

deep.q: Is recycling enough?
deep.why: Recycling sounds like the answer, but only a small share of all plastic ever made has been recycled. Many items can't be recycled at all.
views: Recyclers
Clean, sorted waste can become new products and saves raw materials.
Zero-waste movement
Refuse and reduce first: the best waste is the one never made.
Companies and governments
Some say individuals can't fix it alone; makers must design products to be reused or taken back.
deep.tryit: For one week, before you buy anything, ask: do I need it, can I reuse something instead?

deep.q: Is a banana peel waste?
deep.why: To us it is rubbish; to a worm, a fungus or a compost heap it is food. Whether something is waste depends on who is looking.
views: Composters
Kitchen peels become rich soil in a few weeks.
Circular economy thinkers
Design everything so one process's 'waste' is another's input, like a forest.
Oneness
If nothing in nature is wasted, perhaps 'waste' is only a human idea of separation.
deep.tryit: Start a small compost pot. Each week, write who is 'eating' the peels.

wsd.p: Sort these.
A plastic bag in the ground can last:
The best order is: Refuse, ____, Reuse, Recycle.
Weigh or count one day's waste at home.

topics.name: Living & non-living: is the distinction real?
sub: The usual 'signs of life': moves, breathes, eats, grows, responds, makes babies, gets rid of waste
Tricky cases that break the list: fire (eats, breathes oxygen, grows, spreads), a 100-year-old dormant seed, growing crystals, a plucked flower, a dead leaf, a virus
J.C. Bose: plants respond to touch, injury and poison; he claimed metals also 'tire' and 'recover'
Everything is made of elements forged in stars
Is a handful of soil living or non-living?
topics.summary: We start by sorting things at home into 'alive' and 'not alive' and writing down why. Then we test those reasons on tricky cases. Fire eats, breathes and grows; is it alive? A seed can sit still for 100 years and then sprout; was it alive all that time? Crystals grow. Then we meet J.C. Bose, who built machines sensitive enough to show plants reacting, and who argued that even metals show tiredness and recovery. We end with the honest truth: scientists still do not have one agreed definition of life. NASA's working definition is 'a self-sustaining chemical system capable of evolution', and even that is argued over.
topics.oneness: If the same atoms move from stars to rocks to plants to me, at what moment does something become 'alive'? Is aliveness a line, or a gradient?

topics.summary: We tell Earth's story on a long rope or saree: Earth forms, it is too hot for life, then early on the first tiny cells appear in water, and humans arrive only in the last few millimetres. We look at photos of stromatolites, rocks built layer by layer by microbes over billions of years, some still growing in Australia today. Then we lay out the main ideas scientists have about how life started, and the one honest answer: nobody knows yet. Scientists have made some building blocks of life in a lab, but never life itself.

topics.name: What's common between living and non-living?
sub: Everything is made of atoms; about 90 kinds occur naturally (elements)
The body is mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen
The same carbon is in pencil lead, diamond, bread and you
Atoms are recycled: the water you drink has passed through clouds, rivers, plants and animals
Stars made most elements: 'we are star stuff'
topics.summary: We ask what a rock, a tree and a child have in common, and find that underneath they are built from the same tiny pieces: atoms. Your body is mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, the same elements found in air, water and coal. Carbon in a pencil and carbon in a diamond are the same atom arranged differently. Atoms never wear out; they keep moving between rocks, air, plants and people. Most of them were made inside stars long before Earth existed. So the difference between living and non-living is not in what they are made of, but in how those pieces are arranged and behave.
topics.oneness: If my atoms were once a star and will one day be soil, which part of the journey is 'me'?

topics.name: Materials around me & their properties

Surprising 'materials': is water a material? Tears? Shadow? Sound? Fire?
topics.summary: Children become material detectives: touching, bending, dropping and floating everyday things and describing them with exact words. Float-or-sink predictions surprise them: a heavy steel plate floats when shaped like a bowl, while a tiny pebble sinks. We look closer with a magnifier or phone microscope: salt is little cubes, cloth is woven threads. We dig into soil, see its layers settle in a jar, and learn that one spoonful of good soil contains more living microbes than there are people on Earth, so is soil living? Finally the big puzzle: water and tears are matter, but a shadow is only missing light, sound is a shaking that travels through matter, and fire is hot glowing gas. What counts as 'stuff'?
topics.oneness: Is soil a thing, or a crowd of living beings? Where does the material end and the living begin?

Groups are made by humans, and they keep changing
topics.summary: We meet the big families of life. Plants: we find the parts on a real plant and discover which parts we eat (carrot is a root, potato is a stem, spinach a leaf, cauliflower a flower, rice a seed), then start growing seeds in light and dark to see what plants need. Fungi surprise everyone: mushrooms are not plants, and DNA shows fungi are closer relatives of animals. We sort animals by features (fur, feathers, scales, backbone or not) and place humans honestly among them: we are mammals, we are animals. Finally we see that these groups are human-made boxes: scientists used to call fungi plants, and today most scientists say birds are living dinosaurs.
topics.oneness: Who drew these boxes, and does nature know about them? If a mushroom is more like me than a plant, what does 'like me' mean?

topics.name: Big Bang & the universe
sub: About 13.8 billion years ago the universe was tiny, hot and dense, and began expanding
First atoms: hydrogen and helium
Mass and gravity: gravity pulls matter into clumps → stars, planets, galaxies, clusters
Stars make heavier elements and scatter them when they explode
Black holes; dark matter and dark energy (about 95% of the universe is something we cannot see)
Our planet: about 71% water, 29% land
topics.summary: We tell the biggest story there is. Long ago everything was squeezed into an unimaginably small, hot speck, which grew and is still growing, like dots on a balloon moving apart as it inflates. As it cooled, the first atoms appeared. Mass pulls on mass; that pull is gravity, and gravity gathered gas into stars and stars into galaxies. Stars cook new elements and scatter them when they explode; our Earth, and we, are made from that dust. Then the mysteries: black holes so strong that light cannot escape, and the shocking fact that most of the universe is 'dark' stuff no one has ever seen. We also learn how ideas about gravity changed: Newton said it is a pulling force, and it worked for 200 years; Einstein showed mass bends space and time itself; and today some scientists think even Einstein's idea needs fixing.
topics.oneness: If everything came from one tiny point, is the universe one thing that became many?

topics.summary: We begin with the child's own world: list everything used in one day and trace where it came from. A single breakfast needs farmers, drivers, shopkeepers and cooks; no human lives alone. We ask why humans live in families and groups: like elephants, wolves and ants, we survive by cooperating, and our bodies are wired to bond (a hug really changes brain chemicals). We see that a child in a forest village, a fishing town or a city in another country lives in a different 'world' with different food, work and rules. We play a barter market to see why money was invented. And we ask the old question honestly: are humans naturally selfish or naturally kind? Thinkers disagree.

topics.summary: There is a whole hidden world all around and inside us. We hear how a Dutch cloth-seller, Leeuwenhoek, ground tiny lenses and was the first person to see 'little animals' swimming in a drop of water. Microbes turn milk into curd, make idli batter rise, rot leaves into soil and, through tiny ocean plankton, make about half the oxygen we breathe. Only a few make us sick. We make curd at home and watch yeast blow up a balloon. And we ask whether viruses are alive: they cannot do anything outside a living cell, so scientists still disagree.

topics.summary: Our world of cars, money and roads is only one world. A crow on the same street lives in a different one. Birds see colours we cannot even imagine, including ultraviolet patterns on flowers and feathers. Many feel the Earth's magnetism and use it like a compass to fly thousands of kilometres; the Amur falcon crosses the Arabian Sea on its way from Asia to Africa. Birds have families, neighbours, quarrels and songs, and crows can remember a human face for years. We try to imagine life in a bird's world, and meet a famous question: can we ever truly know what it is like to be another creature?
topics.oneness: If each being lives in its own world, is there one 'real' world, or many?

topics.name: Cycles in the sky & weather

A year: Earth goes around the Sun; seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun
Moon phases: we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half; the Moon makes no light of its own
India's six ritus and the monsoon
Clouds and rain: water evaporates, cools and condenses

topics.summary: With a torch and a ball we discover why day and night happen: the Earth spins, so our side faces the Sun and then turns away. Seasons come from Earth's tilt; most people wrongly think it is about being closer to the Sun. The Moon makes no light of its own; its shape changes because we see different amounts of its sunlit half, and the child keeps a moon diary for a month. We learn India's six ritus, why the monsoon comes, and make a cloud in a jar. We hear how ideas changed: people once believed the Sun went around the Earth; Aryabhata proposed in 499 CE that the Earth spins; Copernicus and Galileo argued the Earth goes around the Sun, and Galileo was put on trial for it.
topics.oneness: Sun, Moon, seasons and my sleep all move in cycles. Am I part of the sky's rhythm?

sub: Push and pull; gravity pulls everything down
The floor pushes back up (normal force); friction; air resistance; water pushes up (buoyancy); magnets
Contact forces are, at heart, electric pushes between electrons; your hand never truly 'touches' the table
Gravity is the exception, a different force
Sound is vibration travelling through air, water and solids; no sound in space
Loud/soft and high/low (pitch); echoes
topics.summary: Children push, pull, drop and float things to feel forces. The surprise: when you sit on a chair, the chair pushes back up, and when you 'touch' anything, its electrons and yours push each other away; atoms never really touch. Air pushes against a falling sheet of paper; water pushes up on a boat. We retell the history of falling: Aristotle said heavy things fall faster, and people believed him for nearly 2000 years until Galileo tested it; Newton explained gravity as a pull; Einstein explained it as bent space. Sound is also a push travelling along: we feel our throat buzz when humming Om, watch rice jump on a drum, and build a cup telephone.
topics.oneness: If nothing ever truly touches, how are we all still connected?

sub: Light sources: Sun, fire, bulbs, fireflies (living light)
We see when light bounces off things into our eyes

Reflection: mirrors, still water

topics.summary: Darkness is not a thing; it is what is left when light is missing. We make shadow puppets and discover shadows grow as hands move closer to the torch. We bounce torchlight off mirrors to hit a target, make rainbows with a glass of water, and learn that white light is all colours mixed, as Newton showed with a prism. A red apple looks red because it bounces red light and swallows the rest. Then the painting surprise: mixing paints makes colours darker, while mixing coloured light makes white. We paint a ball with one light source to see light, shade and shadow. And the deep puzzle: is light a wave or a particle? Scientists argued for centuries and now say it behaves as both, which still puzzles them.
topics.oneness: Is colour in the apple, in the light, or in my mind?

Floods, droughts and dry spells
Wind, storms and cyclones (countries around the Indian Ocean take turns naming them)
Thunder and lightning (light arrives before sound)
Earthquakes and tsunamis (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami)
Snow in the Himalayas
Why the monsoon happens: land heats faster than sea
topics.summary: Nature is always moving water, air and land around. We follow a raindrop through the water cycle, then see what happens when there is too much (flood) or too little (drought). The monsoon happens because land heats faster than the sea, so moist sea air rushes in. We count the seconds between lightning and thunder to tell how far away a storm is. We learn how earthquakes shake the ground and how in 2004 some Andaman island communities reportedly escaped the tsunami using traditional knowledge of the sea. And we ask whether 'natural disasters' are fully natural: building on riverbeds or cutting forests can make floods far worse.
topics.oneness: Rain, rivers and my body's water are the same water. Is a flood something happening to us or with us?

topics.name: Human impact on the environment
sub: Humans change land (forests → farms and cities), air (smoke), water (plastic, sewage) and climate (burning coal and petrol adds carbon dioxide)
Other animals change environments too (elephants, termites, earthworms, beavers), but humans at a huge scale
Good changes: Jadav Payeng planted a whole forest on a river island; the Chipko movement
Are humans part of nature or outside it?
topics.summary: Every living thing changes its surroundings: earthworms make soil, elephants clear paths, termites build towers. Humans do the same, but at a scale that now changes the whole planet's air, water and weather. We walk the neighbourhood spotting human-made changes, catch dust from the air on a sticky card, and feel how a road is hotter than a tree's shade. We meet people who changed things for the better: Jadav Payeng, the 'Forest Man of India', planted a forest bigger than many towns, and the women of the Chipko movement hugged trees to save them. We discuss honestly that people disagree about how fast to change things and which solutions are best.
topics.oneness: If I am part of nature, is damaging nature damaging myself?

The Elephant Whisperers (2022)

topics.name: Waste: reduce & manage
sub: Nature has no waste: a fallen leaf becomes soil
Kinds of waste: wet, dry, hazardous, e-waste
Where waste goes: landfills, burning, recycling, oceans
Plastic can last hundreds of years
Refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle; composting
India's kabadiwala recycling system
topics.summary: In a forest nothing is wasted: leaves, dead animals and dung all become food for something else. Only humans make things nature cannot easily take back, like plastic that lasts for centuries. We find out what our own family throws away in a week, sort it into wet, dry and hazardous, and bury a banana peel, a paper and a plastic bag to dig up after 3 weeks. We meet India's kabadiwalas, who quietly recycle huge amounts, and old habits like turning sarees into quilts. We also learn an uncomfortable fact: only a small part of all plastic ever made has been recycled, and experts argue about whether recycling is the real answer.
topics.oneness: If nature has no waste, is waste a human idea? Can we live like a forest?

res.title: Arvind Gupta Toys: toys from trash

topics.name: Other life inside me
sub: Trillions of microbes live in and on us: roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells
Gut, skin and mouth each have their own communities
They help digest food, make some vitamins and train our defences
Mitochondria, the energy-makers in our cells, were once free-living bacteria
About 8% of our DNA is left over from ancient viruses
topics.summary: You are not just you: you are a walking city. About as many bacterial cells live in and on your body as your own cells (scientists used to say 10 times more, until a 2016 study corrected it). Your gut microbes help digest food and make vitamins; skin microbes guard against germs. Deeper still, the tiny power stations inside every cell, mitochondria, were once separate bacteria that moved in and never left. Lynn Margulis proposed this and was ridiculed for years before scientists accepted it. Even our DNA carries leftover pieces of ancient viruses. So which part is 'me'?
topics.oneness: If half the cells in my body are not 'mine', and my energy comes from ancient bacteria, what is 'I'?

topics.name: My genes
sub: Every cell carries instructions (DNA), like a recipe book
Half from each biological parent; why siblings differ
All life uses the same DNA 'letters'; we share many genes with bananas, flies and mice
Genes are not destiny: food, care and surroundings switch genes on and off
History: Mendel's peas; Rosalind Franklin's photo; Har Gobind Khorana and the genetic code
topics.summary: Inside almost every cell is a long coded message called DNA, a recipe book for building and running a body. We extract real DNA from strawberries and see the white strands. Half our recipes come from each biological parent, mixed in a new way, which is why siblings look alike but different. All living things use the same four DNA letters, so we share many genes even with bananas. We meet Mendel, a monk whose pea experiments were ignored for 34 years; Rosalind Franklin, whose photo revealed DNA's shape but who got little credit; and Har Gobind Khorana, born in Punjab, who won a Nobel Prize for cracking how DNA's code works. And we learn that genes are not destiny: what we eat, how we live and how we are cared for changes which genes are used.
topics.oneness: If a banana and I share the same code, are we written in the same language by the same author?

topics.name: Where humans came from
sub: Life changed over billions of years (evolution): fish → amphibians → reptiles → mammals → primates → humans, a branching tree, not a ladder
Darwin and Wallace: natural selection
Other humans: Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans; Homo sapiens appear about 300,000 years ago in Africa
Many of us carry a little Neanderthal DNA
People reached India tens of thousands of years ago; Bhimbetka rock shelters
topics.summary: We follow our family line back through time: fish that crawled onto land, early mammals scurrying under dinosaurs, tree-climbing primates, and many kinds of humans, several of them alive at the same time. Darwin and Wallace explained how living things slowly change: those best suited to their surroundings survive and pass on their traits. We see that evolution is a branching bush, not a ladder, and that new fossils keep pushing dates back. We visit (in pictures or in person) Bhimbetka's rock paintings, among the oldest human art in India. Then we compare this with the Dashavatara: Matsya (fish), Kurma (tortoise), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (half-lion, half-human), Vamana (small human), then full humans. Many people see in this order a story that parallels evolution.
topics.oneness: If all life is one family tree, is there anyone who is not my relative?

res.title: The Story of Life: Evolution, Catherine Barr & Steve Williams
Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh)

topics.name: What's common between me and other life?
sub: Me & a dog: mammals, backbone, the same organs, hair, milk, feelings
Me & a bird: backbone, lungs, a 4-chambered heart
Me & a fish: backbone; early embryos look alike
Me & a tree: cells, DNA, using energy, water
Me & a mushroom: closer relatives than plants
Me & bacteria: the same DNA code and energy molecule
Differences too
topics.summary: We play detective comparing ourselves with other beings, one at a time. A dog shares our skeleton plan, organs, fur-like hair, milk-feeding and clearly feels joy and fear. A bird has a 4-chambered heart like ours. A tree breathes at the level of its cells, carries DNA and is made of cells like us. Even bacteria run on the same genetic code and energy molecule. The deeper we look, the longer the 'same' list grows. We also hear the 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, in which scientists stated that many animals, including birds and octopuses, are conscious, and the 2024 New York Declaration, which says even insects might be.
topics.oneness: 'Tat tvam asi': you are that. When does 'same' become 'one'?

res.title: My Octopus Teacher (2020)

topics.name: Our closest cousins
sub: Great apes: chimpanzees and bonobos (closest; about 98–99% similar DNA), gorillas, orangutans
Monkeys and other primates
India's only ape: the hoolock gibbon (Northeast)
Shared: tools, emotions, play, laughter, culture
Jane Goodall: chimps use tools
topics.summary: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives; we shared an ancestor several million years ago. When Jane Goodall saw a chimp stripping a twig to fish for termites, scientists had believed tool-making was what made humans unique. Her mentor Louis Leakey said we must now 'redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' Chimps laugh, mourn, make up after fights and have local traditions. India has its own ape, the hoolock gibbon, singing in northeastern forests. We tape our thumbs to see why our hands matter, and ask: what, if anything, makes humans special?
topics.oneness: Every 'only humans can…' claim has been challenged. Is the line between us and them real?

res.title: Jane Goodall documentaries (e.g. Jane, 2017)

topics.name: My family history
sub: Family tree (3 generations); 'family' = the people who raise and love me (inclusive of adopted, single-parent and other families)
Traits that run in families: face, height, hair, handedness
Fingerprints: unique, even for identical twins
Stories, languages, places, recipes
How long people lived then vs now
Blood groups and family illnesses: parent-led and kept light
topics.summary: Every child is the newest page in a very long story. We build a family tree, interview a grandparent or elder, collect photos and stories, and look at what is shared: a nose, a laugh, a love of cooking. We take fingerprints and discover that no two people, not even identical twins, have the same ones. We learn that in 1947 people in India lived on average only about 32 years and now about 70, and ask why. For families that wish to, parents can add blood groups and health stories. Families made by adoption or in other ways trace both their 'raised-by' and 'born-from' stories in whatever way feels right.
topics.oneness: My family tree joins every other family tree if I go back far enough. Where does my family end?

topics.name: My body parts
sub: Skin (the largest organ), bones (about 300 at birth, 206 in adults), muscles, heart, lungs, stomach and intestines, brain
How they work together
Why they evolved: forward eyes, gripping thumbs, sweating for long-distance running, goosebumps from furry ancestors, tailbone
The appendix: once called useless, now possibly a store of helpful microbes
topics.summary: We trace the child's body on a big sheet of paper and place cut-out organs inside. We listen to the heart with a home-made stethoscope before and after jumping, blow up a balloon to feel lung power, and build a moving finger from straws and string. Then we ask 'why do I have this?' Goosebumps are left over from furry ancestors whose hair stood up; sweating lets humans run for hours; babies are born with about 300 bones that fuse to 206. We learn that science changes its mind: the appendix was called useless for a century and now may be a safe house for helpful gut microbes. Finally we meet another way of seeing the body: Sushruta, an early surgeon who described nose reconstruction, and the yoga and Ayurveda traditions that describe the body differently.
topics.oneness: My heart beats without my asking. Is it 'my' heart, or is it doing its own thing?

res.title: Science centres: Nehru Science Centre Mumbai, Visvesvaraya Museum Bengaluru, National Science Centre Delhi

topics.name: My body's sensors
sub: Beyond the 'five senses': touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, itch, balance, body position (eyes closed), hunger, thirst, full tummy, heartbeat, the urge to breathe
Conscious vs automatic sensing
Senses mix: flavour = taste + smell
Other beings: birds (UV, magnetic field), bees (UV), snakes (heat), sharks (electric fields), bats (echoes), dogs (smell)
Plants sense light, gravity and touch
topics.summary: Aristotle listed five senses over 2000 years ago, and people repeated the list ever since. But your body is covered in sensors: you know where your hand is with your eyes closed, you feel hot and cold, you stay balanced on one foot, you feel hungry, thirsty or that you need the toilet, and a hidden sensor makes you breathe faster when you run. Scientists today count anywhere from about 20 to over 30 senses and still disagree on how to count. We pinch our noses and find apple and potato taste almost the same, because most flavour is smell. Then we meet the superpowers of others: snakes 'see' heat, sharks feel electricity, bats hear their way in the dark, birds feel Earth's magnetism. Even plants sense: roots know which way is down and the touch-me-not folds when touched.
topics.oneness: If a plant senses touch and I sense touch, is sensing the beginning of awareness everywhere?

res.title: What If You Had Animal Eyes?, Sandra Markle

topics.name: How do I think?
sub: The brain: about 86 billion neurons sending signals
Thinking = patterns of signals; learning changes connections
Memory: short-term and long-term; sleep helps memory; memories change each time we recall them
Emotions affect thinking
Other thinkers: crows, octopuses; even brainless slime moulds solve mazes
The hard question: how does the brain make experience?
topics.summary: Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells passing tiny electric and chemical signals; every time you learn something new, the connections change. We play memory games and discover tricks that help (stories, pictures, a 'memory palace' walk through the house) and learn that sleep is when the brain files memories. Surprisingly, a memory changes a little each time you remember it. Thinking isn't only human: crows plan, octopuses solve puzzles, and a slime mould with no brain at all can find the shortest path through a maze. Then the biggest mystery: nobody knows how signals in the brain become the feeling of being you. Some scientists say the mind is what the brain does; Vedanta says consciousness comes first and the brain is something that appears within it.
topics.oneness: Who is watching my thoughts? Is the watcher a thought too?

topics.name: Getting sick, getting hurt & getting well
sub: Why we get sick: germs (bacteria, viruses), not enough food or sleep, allergies
The body's defences: skin, mucus, fever, white blood cells, antibodies, immune memory (how vaccines work)
Hygiene habits: handwashing (20 seconds), teeth, bathing, clean water and food, covering coughs
Getting hurt: cuts, burns, falls, electric shock; electricity safety at home
Healing: scabs, rest
Are 'I' and 'my body' different?
topics.summary: We learn that the body is a fortress: skin is the wall, mucus is a sticky trap, fever is the body turning up the heat on germs, and white blood cells are guards who remember invaders so they can fight faster next time (which is how vaccines work). Glitter 'germs' show why handwashing matters, and bread touched by washed vs unwashed hands grows very different mould. We tell the story of Dr Semmelweis, who told doctors to wash their hands in the 1840s and was mocked; years later germ theory proved him right. We learn home safety, especially electricity: water and electricity never mix, never touch sockets or bare wires, and never touch someone being shocked; switch off first. Finally the question: we say 'help my body heal'. Who is helping whom? Am I my body, or something more?
topics.oneness: When I say 'my body', who is the 'I' that owns it?

res.title: Germs Make Me Sick!, Melvin Berger

topics.name: What is food?
sub: Food = building material + energy + helpers (vitamins, minerals) + water
Digestion breaks food down: proteins → amino acids, carbohydrates → sugars, fats → fatty acids
All life uses the same ~20 amino acids, DNA code and energy molecule (ATP)
So why so many foods? Different bodies have different tools (teeth, enzymes, gut microbes)
Plants make their own food from light; food chains
Food for different beings: cows (helped by microbes), spiders, plants, fungi
topics.summary: We chew a piece of plain roti for two minutes and it starts tasting sweet: saliva is already breaking starch into sugar. Digestion is a giant breaking-down factory: proteins become amino acids, carbohydrates become sugars, fats become fatty acids, and the body rebuilds them into itself. Amazingly, every living thing builds itself from the same 20 or so amino acids. So why does a cow eat grass, a spider eat flies and a plant eat sunlight? Because each has different tools: a cow's stomach is full of microbes that break down grass, which we cannot do. We also learn that nutrition science keeps changing its mind: fat was the villain, then sugar, and eggs went from bad to fine.
topics.oneness: 'Annam Brahma': food is the Absolute. When I eat a mango, does the mango become me, or do I become a little more mango?

topics.name: Energy beyond food
sub: Sunlight: plants make sugar from light (photosynthesis); we make vitamin D in sunlight; warmth
Air: oxygen helps cells release energy from food; we breathe out carbon dioxide
Water: most of the body is water; every cell works in it
Life without sunlight: deep-sea vents where bacteria make food from chemicals (chemosynthesis); tubeworms
Microbes that 'breathe' nitrate or sulphate instead of oxygen; life in boiling springs, ice and deep rock
Tardigrades survive extremes
topics.summary: Food is only one kind of fuel. Plants catch sunlight and turn it into sugar; that sugar feeds almost everything else, including us. Our cells use oxygen to release energy from food, like a slow fire, and we breathe out carbon dioxide. A plant left in a dark box turns pale, and a candle under a jar goes out when its oxygen runs low. Then we dive to the deep ocean floor, where no sunlight has ever reached, and find whole communities living on chemicals from hot volcanic vents. Some microbes breathe sulphate instead of oxygen, some live in boiling water or deep inside rocks, and tiny tardigrades can survive drying out and even the vacuum of space. Life is far stranger and more flexible than the textbook picture.
topics.oneness: If all my energy started as sunlight, am I a little bit of the Sun, walking around?
